They don't look like they will be able to navigate things like steps, or the terrible layout and infrastructure in many U.S. cities. This includes broken sidewalks, no sidewalks (a biggy in many places), or the long distances they would have to travel to get to most peoples homes.

Nor do they look like they would work properly in most snow, ice, or handle street flooding very well. It's great in concept, but it doesn't seem so great in practice.

I guess I could see this in selective urban environments, but not most urban/suburban settings. Many U.S. cities just aren't set up for this type of device, especially when you consider that they would have to operate on streets to get from retail areas to most residential areas.

For instance, although there are small convenience stores and some mom and pop grocery stores in my city, the vast majority of larger retailers, the type that would use something like this, are in commercial areas away from most residential locations. Something like this would work for a very small portion of my city (very small)--and I live in a pretty standard U.S. city. Companies would have to go out of their way to develop delivery substations to make it work.

Snow you are so right on that. That's a good point. It strikes me as a solution that's looking for a problem.
That is a good way of putting it.

The chain grocery stores in my city are all doing delivery now, as well as, "we'll get it off the shelf and you come pick it up" It's pointlessly expensive for the delivery though, I could see these working for that purpose. As for snow and Ice, I could see it working with different tires or tracks or something. I agree that this early prototype won't be able to handle every situation, but I think it would be useful enough that some companies would adopt them.

As to the headline about them beating airborne drones, that part I definitely agree with, not having to deal with getting permission from the FAA removes a huge obstacle.

Proper tires might help, but part of the problem isn't tires, it is the fact that for many northern locations, mountainous regions, parts of the Midwest, and a big section of the East Coast, sidewalks aren't even available during certain winter months--they are covered in thick ice and snow, plowed over, and/or blocked by obstructions. And this doesn't even address them getting from retailers to residential areas, places that are often times not connected by sidewalks--which isn't going to happen with a range that only takes it 2 miles from the store.

I'm not saying that something like this doesn't have potential, but at this point, with its current capabilities, it isn't going to be doing much for 99% of the U.S. population. They would have to create a street legal autonomous robot with a more realistic range that is capable of going much further, and that operates in much more challenging environments, especially if it is going to make multiple trips in a short period of time without having to recharge and/or replace the battery every trip it makes--something that would be cost prohibitive.

And although they don't have to worry about the FAA, they do have to worry about getting approval to use autonomous vehicles on public streets, and most cities don't even have that on their radar yet.
